text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to the Health Report with me, Norman
Swan. Today, having a hip or knee replacement when you are relatively young.
What should you know?

Surprising genetic findings in women with endometriosis which could change the
treatment.

And we will follow up last week's story on outdoor temperatures and the chances
of developing gestational diabetes in a minute.

A hormone that is commonly used to speed up labour turns out to have quite
profound effects on the brain and behaviour. The hormone is called oxytocin, and
when given by a nasal spray to children with autism in a trial at the Brain and
Mind Centre at the University of Sydney, it showed significant benefits in their
behaviour. Those findings have launched a series of international collaborations
which hold a lot of hope for children with autism. Professor Adam Guastella, who
is one of the research leaders at the Brain and Mind Centre, is in our Sydney
studio. Welcome.

Adam Guastella: Welcome Norman.

Norman Swan: So just tell us, oxytocin, which causes the uterus to contract, is
involved in orgasm and things like that, involved in behaviour?

Adam Guastella: Well, let me just start with autism first actually. As you're no
doubt aware, autism is a neurodevelopmental disability that weakens one's ability
to process and respond accurately to social relationships and social information.
So people with autism can often be seen to have difficulty with eye gaze and
recognising emotion and expressing one's own emotions and understanding the
nuances of social information. That often gets worse as the information becomes
more complex, such as group situations. And there's a brain process underlying
some of these developments, and we are starting to understand some of the
brain processes that are really underpinning these difficulties.

Norman Swan: So, oxytocin?

Adam Guastella: So oxytocin is a hormone and a neuropeptide, and there has
been 30 years of research demonstrating…
 
Norman Swan: Neuropeptide meaning a short protein, which you're suggesting
acts as a messenger in the brain, rather than a traditional hormone.

Adam Guastella: Yes, that's right. And we know that when…I'll just go straight to
the neurobiological research, that oxytocin facilitates communication, in particular
facilitates the processing of social information. So it seems to facilitate the
processing of faces, memory for faces, ability to respond to faces accurately.
We've conducted over 10 years of research in humans showing that when we
administer the nasal spray, it improves things like eye gaze, emotion recognition
and memory for social information.

Norman Swan: In non-autistic people?

Adam Guastella: In students that we've tested, as well as people with autism
who are adults.

Norman Swan: So tell me about this trial you did?

Adam Guastella: We had spent 10 years studying the potential of the treatment
and then we administered oxytocin morning and night for five weeks to young
children with autism aged between three and eight years of age.

Norman Swan: So these are kids with serious communication disorders,
intellectual disabilities and so on, the full bit, not at the other end of the autism
spectrum where they might just have some communication problems.

Adam Guastella: Absolutely. Autism is a spectrum, they all met what we call the
diagnosis of autism, and some were more severe than others. But they all met
the diagnosis. But we certainly didn't just select those that were not severe,
which is common in a lot of research. So with these children, we asked
caregivers to give the oxytocin morning and night, and we also asked the
caregivers at a separate time to give placebo morning and night for five weeks.
And what we found…

Norman Swan: And they didn't know it was a placebo.

Adam Guastella: No one knew, so it was a double-blind, randomised trial. And
what we found was that when children receive the oxytocin they were more
responsive, they were better able to respond to their caregivers, caregivers
 
noticed this social engagement or increased social engagement. And even when
they came into the laboratory when we did our social testing, the experimenters
in our research study who didn't know who received what also reported that the
children under oxytocin showed improved social behaviour.

Norman Swan: And oxytocin doesn't last long in the blood, so when they
stopped it, they went back to where they were?

Adam Guastella: This is speaking to the mechanism. So it's really very, very
interesting. In this study when people stop the oxytocin treatment they went back
to where they were, that's correct. But what we think oxytocin can do is open up
a window of opportunity to teach social skills and social rules for young children
so they can respond more effectively to early intervention.

Norman Swan: I think you're doing a study now with Duke University in North
Carolina where you are combining oxytocin with an intensive training program.

Adam Guastella: Yes, that's right, so presently the best treatment for autism in
young children is social learning therapies, like the Early Start Denver Model.
And these therapies are most effective when provided to young children aged
between two and five.

Norman Swan: And they've been credited with stopping the stereotypic
behaviour of the kid in the corner banging their head and that sort of thing, but
they really try and bring a child back into mainstream.

Adam Guastella: That's right, they can be more socially engaged, and in some
ways find the social experience a lot more enjoyable. Some children respond to
these therapies and some don't. They get reasonably good outcomes. But all
children in Australia should have access to those therapies, but we need to
improve response. And so what we are doing now is we are looking at if we
combine these very critical windows of opportunity with oxytocin treatment and
enhance the learning, whether that produces a stronger response.

Norman Swan: And what about at the…I'd hesitate to call it the milder end. I
always get told by people who deal with autism that you shouldn't call it the
milder end because it can be very disabling…but kids who are more engaged
and less disabled by their autism, does oxytocin help them, do we know?
 
Adam Guastella: Well, the focus of our research is on helping people that want
the treatment. We know that in people at the higher end, oxytocin improves
social responsiveness and improves their ability to understand social cues. But
really where we want to go to is that if treatments are effective we want to be
able to provide those treatments. And when they stop being effective we need to
be able to know, we need to be able to see that those treatments are no longer
effective and switch them to something else.

Norman Swan: What about cost?

Adam Guastella: It's currently under research, so it's not something that is
administered widely under drug companies in Australia. But as the research
develops it's something that is regarded as a generic and could be widely
available to Australians.

Norman Swan: And side-effects?

Adam Guastella: So the research needs to be conducted…I'd never suggest
anyone start using oxytocin now, but in the studies we've conducted there has
been no long-term side-effects that we've identified at this point.

Norman Swan: You get problems with excess urination and things like that.

Adam Guastella: So in small numbers, say three of our participants we noticed
excess urination.

Norman Swan: And briefly, some people…you know, it's kind of the thing of the
moment, so people are suggesting oxytocin as an anxiety drug and other things.
Can you comment on that, how widely this could be used?

Adam Guastella: Well, the mechanisms of oxytocin are important. So it
improves your ability to process social information. And so for people who might
be anxious in social situations they've started to ask, well, can we use oxytocin
for that purpose? It doesn't have a strong anxiolytic property. So in the doses that
we provide we don't see very strong anxiolytic effects. But it has been proposed
as a potential treatment for a range of problems I guess.

Norman Swan: So when you have the results from your American collaboration
you might have, as you say, a useful lever to help these kids and their families.
 
Adam Guastella: Yes, I think the key really is that we need to be able to do the
large trials here in Sydney and develop the evidence so that people can have the
option of using these sorts of treatments in the future.

Norman Swan: Adam, thanks very much for coming in to join us on the Health
Report.

Adam Guastella: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Adam Guastella from the Brain and Mind Centre at the
University of Sydney.

Let's go to that follow-up to last week's story…you're listening, by the way, to
the Health Report here on RN, ABC news and CBC radio across Canada, and
I'm Norman Swan.

So last week we had a story on outdoor temperatures and the chances of
developing gestational diabetes, pregnancy induced diabetes. It was a Canadian
study which effectively showed a doubling of the prevalence between the depths
of winter and the heat of summer in Toronto. The explanation was that the cold of
winter induced brown fat which burned calories and made insulin work better in
these women. Well, there's been a similar Australian study which has made
equivalent findings in terms of seasonality of pregnancy, but the researchers
reckon there's a more mundane but still a significant explanation. I have one of
them on the line from Wollongong in New South Wales, Professor Bob Moses
who is director of diabetes services there. Welcome to the Health Report.

Robert Moses: Thank you Norman.

Norman Swan: So, just briefly, the study and what you found.

Robert Moses: Well, it goes back more than 20 years. We did an original study
looking at the potential seasonality of gestational problems, using then the
current criteria for the diagnosis. We found that the glucose levels after the
challenge went up, but not enough to cause any change in the prevalence.

We subsequently went on to do a work with a climate chamber with the
University of Wollongong. We put otherwise healthy people into a climate
chamber and gave them a GTT, a glucose tolerance test. We found quite a
 
dramatic increase in the one and two hour glucose levels between 25 and 30
degrees. So that has been a bit quiet now for some time. And then because the
criteria for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes has changed relatively recently…

Norman Swan: In other words, they've lowered the threshold, it's easier to
diagnose it in some ways, easier to qualify.

Robert Moses: Yes or over-diagnosis perhaps, who knows. But certainly the
criteria have changed and there is now a greater prevalence. So we decided
to…and that's why it must be correct, like most things we do, the nurses told us
first they were having troubles coping with the workload…

Norman Swan: Always listen to the nurses.

Robert Moses: Yes, they were having troubles coping with the workload…

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Robert Moses: Well, we looked at the criteria prospectively, the number of
patients, and we found that it was a marked variation in the prevalence between
winter and summer.

Norman Swan: With more being in summer.

Robert Moses: Yes. So compared to the autumn or spring there was about 25%
more women with abnormal results in summer, and 25% less in winter. So the
overall variation was about 50%.

Norman Swan: So the Canadian said, well, the reason for that is probably that
you are making insulin more efficient in winter because you are producing more
brown fat, but you don't agree with that conclusion.

Robert Moses: I don't think any of us have got down that far as to what the
possible reason is. Certainly, as I mentioned before, with a climate chamber and
controlling the ambient temperature from 20 through to 35 degrees there was a
dramatic increase in the glucose levels, not the fasting but the one and two hour
levels, starting at 25 to 30 degrees.
 
Norman Swan: But you think it could be a mistake in the way you are
measuring…not a mistake but an aberration in the way blood is shunted around
the body that might produce the result.

Robert Moses: As you say, it's not a mistake. The actual rise in the glucose level
was correlated with the core temperature. And what happens as you get a hotter
environment is that you tend to divert more blood from the arterial side to the
venous side so you can help to lose heat through the skin.

Norman Swan: And why should that affect your blood sugar?

Robert Moses: Because there's more glucose in the arterial side than in the
venous side because it hasn't gone through the small arterioles and things.

Norman Swan: So in other words what you are suggesting and what I saw in
your paper is that you could actually be over-diagnosing in summer. So it's not so
much that there's more gestational diabetes, it's just that the way you do the test
in that hotter temperature could actually give you a false positive result.

Robert Moses: Or a false negative in winter. So there is a 50% range…

Norman Swan: Not very comforting, Professor Moses.

Robert Moses: Well, we are about to embark with a climate chamber again,
looking at how long you have to be at a certain temperature before you don't
have this problem. It might be two hours or three hours, but that of course could
be a First World problem. You have to have air conditioning, et cetera. On the
other hand, if you go to places where this is not practical, you may have to devise
a correction factor to try and work out what the proper GTT…

Norman Swan: So what's a pregnant woman to do in the interim while you are
working it out?

Robert Moses: Well, I think that she should have her normal GTT at about 24 to
26 weeks, and then possibly discuss the results with whoever is looking after her.

Norman Swan: And work it out from there. We're sure to have you on when
you've got some more results from your chamber. Otherwise we can rest in our
 
belief, for the moment anyway, that brown fat may actually help you. Thanks for
joining us.

Robert Moses: It's a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Professor Bob Moses is director of the diabetes service at
Illawarra and Shoalhaven local health district. That's based in Wollongong.

Endometriosis is an incredibly common problem in women during their
childbearing years. It's hard to treat, causes infertility and a lot of pain. Here's
Olivia's story. It took nine years for Olivia to be diagnosed.

Olivia: First odd occurrence was getting my period at 10 years old, which is quite
young. It was around about when I was 14 that I started to notice that I was
suffering a lot more than the girls in my school. I thought maybe I was a bit of a
sook because I realised that I was having to take time off school and I was
bleeding for a lot longer and I was getting a lot of iron issues. My friends would
come up to me at school and say, oh, exercise really helps for period cramps.
And the first thing I thought was the last thing I can do at that time of the month is
exercise. I can't move, I can't get out of bed, and that's when I started to think
that there was something wrong.

So I had started going to the doctors as soon as I got heavy periods, they were
always saying, no, it's totally normal, it's fine, I'm sure it's not that bad, I'm sure
it's just a bad month. And I just listened to them as a young girl wanting to fix the
issue rather than create more issues. But it wasn't until early last year that I got
extraordinarily bad and the pains were insane and I started fainting quite
regularly and bled for about 10 weeks at a time. And I thought no, this isn't
normal. And so I pushed and pushed at several doctors, and finally got referred
to a gynaecologist who agreed and said, yes, you sound like textbook
endometriosis.

Then you need to have an operation to formally diagnose it, which is called a
laparoscopy. And you can choose a surgeon who is either an excision specialist
or just a regular gynaecologist. I would recommend an excision specialist
because they know how to look for endometriosis. And if it is, then usually during
that operation they will cut it out or burn it, called excision or ablation, and go
 
from there, which is hormone therapy or a plethora of other options, depending
on what your gynaecologist suggests.

Norman Swan: Olivia, who spoke to Joel Werner. As a result of recent genetic
research there are some women with endometriosis who may have more
effective options. For a condition with a very low risk of cancer, a North American
group has found surprisingly a set of cancer genes in endometriosis legions. One
of the team was Paul Yong who is a gynaecologist who specialises in
endometriosis at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver.

Paul Yong: One in 10 women of reproductive age have endometriosis, that's
approximately 1 million women in Canada.

Norman Swan: And 50% of women who have infertility have endometriosis.

Paul Yong: Yes, approximately half the women with infertility, approximately half
of women with troublesome pelvic pain have endometriosis.

Norman Swan: So how does a woman know she's got endometriosis? What's
the story?

Paul Yong: The symptoms include painful menstrual cramps, also painful sexual
activity, painful bowel movements, the latter often are worse at the time of the
period. There can also be pained that is there are even daily. And then a history
of infertility can often be suggested.

Norman Swan: And the pain is mostly in the pelvis?

Paul Yong: Mostly in the pelvis, yes.

Norman Swan: And what's going on here is that tissue from the uterus, from the
womb, gets seeded throughout the pelvis and sometimes throughout the bowel.

Paul Yong: Yes.

Norman Swan: And we don't know very much about it apart from the fact that
once a woman goes through menopause it tends to go away.

Paul Yong: That is correct, yes, it seems to be an oestrogen dependent disease.
 
Norman Swan: And where are we at with treatment for endometriosis? Because
there is not just one type.

Paul Yong: Treatment is primarily hormonal or surgical. Hormonal includes
progestin based therapies such as the birth control pill, or progesterone only
treatments. And then surgery involves excision or ablation of legions, or
hysterectomy.

Norman Swan: And there are mainly two kinds of lesion here with
endometriosis, aren't there, ones which are a bit superficial and attach to tissues,
and a type where it really burrows into the organ that it attaches itself to, which is
a bit like cancer except that it's not cancer.

Paul Yong: Correct, that's exactly it. The latter type has tumour-like qualities but
is most definitely benign and extremely rare for the deep infiltrating type of
endometriosis to be associated with cancer.

Norman Swan: Is there any relationship at all between endometriosis and
cancer?

Paul Yong: There is a relationship that appears with endometriosis that grows on
the ovary, which is the third subtype of endometriosis and certain subtypes of
ovarian cancer. It's about a 2 to 4 fold increase in risk. But because
endometriosis is so common, only a very tiny fraction of women with
endometriosis develop cancer.

Norman Swan: And what do we know about what causes it or the risk factors
that put a woman at risk of endometriosis?

Paul Yong: There seems to be some factors based on ethnicity, for example,
and there are gene changes that one inherits that could potentially be dietary
factors or other environmental factors…

Norman Swan: Such as?

Paul Yong: A lot of them are not in a total confirmed state, so I would hesitate to
say for sure.

Norman Swan: And the ethnic groups?
 
Paul Yong: It's thought that Caucasians may have a higher rate of
endometriosis.

Norman Swan: So this was a genetic study. You talked about inherited genes
there that might put you at added risk, but this is a study not of inherited genes
but of the genes that might be mutated in women with endometriosis, particularly
of this deep infiltrating kind, it's something new to the endometriosis itself.

Paul Yong: Yes.

Norman Swan: A small study, but tell us briefly what he found.

Paul Yong: What we found is that this subtype of endometriosis, the cells
contain gene changes or mutations in certain genes that have been seen to be
involved in a certain type of cancer. So these are gene mutations that are
thought to drive cancer cell growth or invasion. So we found these same gene
mutations in endometriosis, the deep infiltrating subtype. So again, this subtype
is very rare to become cancer, so what we think is that these gene mutations
may be driving how endometriosis cells can grow or become invasive in some
areas, and that could fundamentally change management.

Norman Swan: There's quite a spread though in these mutations, it wasn't
consistent, it wasn't the same mutation in every woman.

Paul Yong: Correct, yes, different between individuals.

Norman Swan: Why might that be?

Paul Yong: That's a really good question. It's not completely clear. I think one
factor is that the technologies for detecting these mutations are evolving, and we
think that there will be even more mutations detected with more sensitive
techniques. The other factor is that although there are several different genes
seen, all of them potentially confer an advantage on the cells to be able to grow.

Norman Swan: In cancer, you get these mutations because of environmental
factors…sorry to keep on coming back to this. So, for example, in melanoma
where some of these mutations occur, it's sunlight. In colon cancer it could be red
meat or toxins in the bowel. In the lung it can be tobacco smoke or unknown
 
environmental factors. It's going to be an environmental factor that induces these
mutations in the endometriosis, surely?

Paul Yong: Yes, I think that is a fantastic point and I think definitely more work is
needed to find these environmental factors that are involved in mutations or
healthy cells and mutations survive longer. There's a different study that looked
at some other benign conditions that carry these type of mutations and they
found that age, so increased age was a factor, and I believe smoking was also a
factor. But I don't think that can be extrapolated to endometriosis but I think…

Norman Swan: No, because it's a young woman's disease. And finally, at least
one of these mutations, the KRAS gene, has drugs which are available to treat it
if it's cancer. Surely it's worth trying those on endometriosis, isn't it?

Paul Yong: Yes, there is definitely a lot of potential there for sure. The KRAS
iteration, as far as I know, it's been a somewhat difficult target. So the drugs look
at I believe downstream targets of the KRAS gene. But we would be very
interested in the endometriosis that carries this mutation for specific drugs and
increase the number of treatment options for women.

Norman Swan: So a woman listening to this will wonder should she ask for gene
testing if she's got endometriosis. Is there any point at the moment?

Paul Yong: At this point we don't know the full clinical implications of these gene
mutations, so we are actively working on that right now to see whether these
mutations influence pain levels or infertility, or where endometriosis grows, for
example, or whether a woman will respond to hormonal treatment or surgery. So
all of those are unknowns right now. And until we know that, mutation testing
would be just part of our research protocol.

Norman Swan: Paul Yong, thank you very much for joining us on the Health
Report.

Paul Yong: Thank you very much for having me.

Norman Swan: Paul Yong is in the BC Women's Centre for Pelvic Pain and
Endometriosis in Vancouver.
 
Hip and knee replacements for arthritis are, in the right circumstances, highly
effective operations. They can restore mobility and reduce pain. And because of
that, joint replacement surgery is increasingly being used in younger men and
women. The big question though is whether by having a joint replacement at a
younger age you increase your chances of needing it to be revised. In other
words, a repeat operation, which the evidence suggests is rarely as good as the
first operation.

There is a register of joint replacements in Australia, but it and other national
registries have not been good at estimating the lifetime risk of joint revision, and
that's what a study published recently in the Lancet has done, looking at the
effect of age at first total joint replacement on the risk of subsequent revision.
The first author was orthopaedic surgeon Lee Bayliss of the University of Oxford.
Welcome to the Health Report.

Lee Bayliss: Thank you for having me.

Norman Swan: Just tell us about the study, because it was pretty big.

Lee Bayliss: Yes, so this is based on a primary care dataset which includes
something in the region of 6 million patients. And so within that we had access to
just over 120,000 patients who had had a first time hip or knee replacement, and
that was over a period of approximately 20 years.

Norman Swan: As opposed to, say, the Australian National Joint Replacement
Registry which goes for a year or maybe 10 years, so it's a much longer period of
time.

Lee Bayliss: Yes, sure, and similarly with our own national registry which is over
10 years now by some way but still limited to that time period. So the benefit of
this study was having a more protracted time course to follow these patients that
had these joint replacements and to be able to see what variations there were in
terms of how quickly and at what time following their first procedure they needed
to have that joint replacement really replaced, as you say, a revision procedure.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?
 
Lee Bayliss: What we found was that the extremes of age, so about 15% each
of patients having joint replacements are under 60 and over 80, so those two
groups together constitute about a third of patients, and they displayed very
different behaviours. So I think the most important thing really is that the patients
over 70, in both men and women and hip and knee replacements, the chances of
requiring a second operation within your lifespan were 5%, something in the
region of one in 20.

Norman Swan: If you're over 70.

Lee Bayliss: If you're over 70. And then by contrast of that, if you are under 60,
and particularly the youngest age group, the 50 to 54 age group, there is a
significant increase in the risk of a requirement for a second operation…

Norman Swan: Sorry, we lost you for a moment there. So the 50 year group,
what was their revisionary…?

Lee Bayliss: Yes, 50 to 54, that was the highest risk of revision for both men and
women, significantly more so in men where the revision risk went up something
like one in three, and around 35% for men having knee replacements and a little
bit less for men having hip replacements. But significantly less for women but still
the highest risk for women was in the youngest age groups.

Norman Swan: And you found that the median time to revision for patients who
had surgery younger than 60 was 4.4 years.

Lee Bayliss: Yes, we did…

Norman Swan: So is that in that 30% who needed a revision, or overall?

Lee Bayliss: That's a function of the population. So yes, as you say, of those
people that needed revision, they had it within that time period. But what we also
found is when we looked at something called the hazard function, so the chance
of you needing a revision at any given point in time, so whatever number of days
or years following your surgery, your risk at that point in time of requiring a
second operation, what we found was that was consistently higher in the in the
youngest patients, be they male or female, hip or knee replacement patients. And
I think previously we probably would have not expected that to necessarily have
 
been the case consistently throughout the course of those younger patients, but
that's what our data showed.

Norman Swan: We are running out of time, so just very brief questions. Not
much difference between hips and knees, knees a bit worse than the hips
basically you found, is that right?

Lee Bayliss: No, hips are slightly worse than knees overall.

Norman Swan: Oh really? Why men more than women in the other group?

Lee Bayliss: Really difficult to answer. The honest answer is that wasn't in the
scope of the study, and I can speculate that the traditional reasons that people
give tends to be to do with body weight and profession. But again, that
speculation rather than anything we looked into in this study.

Norman Swan: What the Australian register has shown is that the older hip joints
and the cheaper ones have been the most reliable ones and the newer ones less
reliable. Did you find any cohort effect? There's been some spectacularly
unreliable hip joints. Did you find any difference by year?

Lee Bayliss: No. We did look. What we did not have was data on the proprietary
implants. I imagine you're talking about metal or metal implants. We didn't have
any information about specific types of implants, it was just total hip or a total
knee. Looking across the time periods, the revision rates for both hip and knee
were relatively uniform.

Norman Swan: So the message is, Lee, 'hang on if you can'.

Lee Bayliss: Well, that's difficult to answer because obviously this is looking at a
population, not an individual patient's course through those ages. I think it's just
important that patients enter into discussion about whether they're going to have
a joint replacement or not are fully versed as best they can be in the risks of that
procedure.

Norman Swan: Lee Bayliss of the University of Oxford, thanks very much for
joining us.

Lee Bayliss: Thank you.
 
Norman Swan: Lee Bayliss is in the department of orthopaedics, rheumatology
and musculoskeletal science at the University of Oxford. I'm Norman Swan, this
has been the Health Report, hope to see you next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to the Health Report with me, Norman
Swan. Today, having a hip or knee replacement when you are relatively young.
What should you know?

Surprising genetic findings in women with endometriosis which could change the
treatment.

And we will follow up last week's story on outdoor temperatures and the chances
of developing gestational diabetes in a minute.

A hormone that is commonly used to speed up labour turns out to have quite
profound effects on the brain and behaviour. The hormone is called oxytocin, and
when given by a nasal spray to children with autism in a trial at the Brain and
Mind Centre at the University of Sydney, it showed significant benefits in their
behaviour. Those findings have launched a series of international collaborations
which hold a lot of hope for children with autism. Professor Adam Guastella, who
is one of the research leaders at the Brain and Mind Centre, is in our Sydney
studio. Welcome.

Adam Guastella: Welcome Norman.

Norman Swan: So just tell us, oxytocin, which causes the uterus to contract, is
involved in orgasm and things like that, involved in behaviour?

Adam Guastella: Well, let me just start with autism first actually. As you're no
doubt aware, autism is a neurodevelopmental disability that weakens one's ability
to process and respond accurately to social relationships and social information.
So people with autism can often be seen to have difficulty with eye gaze and
recognising emotion and expressing one's own emotions and understanding the
nuances of social information. That often gets worse as the information becomes
more complex, such as group situations. And there's a brain process underlying
some of these developments, and we are starting to understand some of the
brain processes that are really underpinning these difficulties.

Norman Swan: So, oxytocin?

Adam Guastella: So oxytocin is a hormone and a neuropeptide, and there has
been 30 years of research demonstrating…

Norman Swan: Neuropeptide meaning a short protein, which you're suggesting
acts as a messenger in the brain, rather than a traditional hormone.

Adam Guastella: Yes, that's right. And we know that when…I'll just go straight to
the neurobiological research, that oxytocin facilitates communication, in particular
facilitates the processing of social information. So it seems to facilitate the
processing of faces, memory for faces, ability to respond to faces accurately.
We've conducted over 10 years of research in humans showing that when we
administer the nasal spray, it improves things like eye gaze, emotion recognition
and memory for social information.

Norman Swan: In non-autistic people?

Adam Guastella: In students that we've tested, as well as people with autism
who are adults.

Norman Swan: So tell me about this trial you did?

Adam Guastella: We had spent 10 years studying the potential of the treatment
and then we administered oxytocin morning and night for five weeks to young
children with autism aged between three and eight years of age.

Norman Swan: So these are kids with serious communication disorders,
intellectual disabilities and so on, the full bit, not at the other end of the autism
spectrum where they might just have some communication problems.

Adam Guastella: Absolutely. Autism is a spectrum, they all met what we call the
diagnosis of autism, and some were more severe than others. But they all met
the diagnosis. But we certainly didn't just select those that were not severe,
which is common in a lot of research. So with these children, we asked
caregivers to give the oxytocin morning and night, and we also asked the
caregivers at a separate time to give placebo morning and night for five weeks.
And what we found…

Norman Swan: And they didn't know it was a placebo.

Adam Guastella: No one knew, so it was a double-blind, randomised trial. And
what we found was that when children receive the oxytocin they were more
responsive, they were better able to respond to their caregivers, caregivers

noticed this social engagement or increased social engagement. And even when
they came into the laboratory when we did our social testing, the experimenters
in our research study who didn't know who received what also reported that the
children under oxytocin showed improved social behaviour.

Norman Swan: And oxytocin doesn't last long in the blood, so when they
stopped it, they went back to where they were?

Adam Guastella: This is speaking to the mechanism. So it's really very, very
interesting. In this study when people stop the oxytocin treatment they went back
to where they were, that's correct. But what we think oxytocin can do is open up
a window of opportunity to teach social skills and social rules for young children
so they can respond more effectively to early intervention.

Norman Swan: I think you're doing a study now with Duke University in North
Carolina where you are combining oxytocin with an intensive training program.

Adam Guastella: Yes, that's right, so presently the best treatment for autism in
young children is social learning therapies, like the Early Start Denver Model.
And these therapies are most effective when provided to young children aged
between two and five.

Norman Swan: And they've been credited with stopping the stereotypic
behaviour of the kid in the corner banging their head and that sort of thing, but
they really try and bring a child back into mainstream.

Adam Guastella: That's right, they can be more socially engaged, and in some
ways find the social experience a lot more enjoyable. Some children respond to
these therapies and some don't. They get reasonably good outcomes. But all
children in Australia should have access to those therapies, but we need to
improve response. And so what we are doing now is we are looking at if we
combine these very critical windows of opportunity with oxytocin treatment and
enhance the learning, whether that produces a stronger response.

Norman Swan: And what about at the…I'd hesitate to call it the milder end. I
always get told by people who deal with autism that you shouldn't call it the
milder end because it can be very disabling…but kids who are more engaged
and less disabled by their autism, does oxytocin help them, do we know?

Adam Guastella: Well, the focus of our research is on helping people that want
the treatment. We know that in people at the higher end, oxytocin improves
social responsiveness and improves their ability to understand social cues. But
really where we want to go to is that if treatments are effective we want to be
able to provide those treatments. And when they stop being effective we need to
be able to know, we need to be able to see that those treatments are no longer
effective and switch them to something else.

Norman Swan: What about cost?

Adam Guastella: It's currently under research, so it's not something that is
administered widely under drug companies in Australia. But as the research
develops it's something that is regarded as a generic and could be widely
available to Australians.

Norman Swan: And side-effects?

Adam Guastella: So the research needs to be conducted…I'd never suggest
anyone start using oxytocin now, but in the studies we've conducted there has
been no long-term side-effects that we've identified at this point.

Norman Swan: You get problems with excess urination and things like that.

Adam Guastella: So in small numbers, say three of our participants we noticed
excess urination.

Norman Swan: And briefly, some people…you know, it's kind of the thing of the
moment, so people are suggesting oxytocin as an anxiety drug and other things.
Can you comment on that, how widely this could be used?

Adam Guastella: Well, the mechanisms of oxytocin are important. So it
improves your ability to process social information. And so for people who might
be anxious in social situations they've started to ask, well, can we use oxytocin
for that purpose? It doesn't have a strong anxiolytic property. So in the doses that
we provide we don't see very strong anxiolytic effects. But it has been proposed
as a potential treatment for a range of problems I guess.

Norman Swan: So when you have the results from your American collaboration
you might have, as you say, a useful lever to help these kids and their families.

Adam Guastella: Yes, I think the key really is that we need to be able to do the
large trials here in Sydney and develop the evidence so that people can have the
option of using these sorts of treatments in the future.

Norman Swan: Adam, thanks very much for coming in to join us on the Health
Report.

Adam Guastella: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Adam Guastella from the Brain and Mind Centre at the
University of Sydney.

Let's go to that follow-up to last week's story…you're listening, by the way, to
the Health Report here on RN, ABC news and CBC radio across Canada, and
I'm Norman Swan.

So last week we had a story on outdoor temperatures and the chances of
developing gestational diabetes, pregnancy induced diabetes. It was a Canadian
study which effectively showed a doubling of the prevalence between the depths
of winter and the heat of summer in Toronto. The explanation was that the cold of
winter induced brown fat which burned calories and made insulin work better in
these women. Well, there's been a similar Australian study which has made
equivalent findings in terms of seasonality of pregnancy, but the researchers
reckon there's a more mundane but still a significant explanation. I have one of
them on the line from Wollongong in New South Wales, Professor Bob Moses
who is director of diabetes services there. Welcome to the Health Report.

Robert Moses: Thank you Norman.

Norman Swan: So, just briefly, the study and what you found.

Robert Moses: Well, it goes back more than 20 years. We did an original study
looking at the potential seasonality of gestational problems, using then the
current criteria for the diagnosis. We found that the glucose levels after the
challenge went up, but not enough to cause any change in the prevalence.

We subsequently went on to do a work with a climate chamber with the
University of Wollongong. We put otherwise healthy people into a climate
chamber and gave them a GTT, a glucose tolerance test. We found quite a

dramatic increase in the one and two hour glucose levels between 25 and 30
degrees. So that has been a bit quiet now for some time. And then because the
criteria for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes has changed relatively recently…

Norman Swan: In other words, they've lowered the threshold, it's easier to
diagnose it in some ways, easier to qualify.

Robert Moses: Yes or over-diagnosis perhaps, who knows. But certainly the
criteria have changed and there is now a greater prevalence. So we decided
to…and that's why it must be correct, like most things we do, the nurses told us
first they were having troubles coping with the workload…

Norman Swan: Always listen to the nurses.

Robert Moses: Yes, they were having troubles coping with the workload…

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Robert Moses: Well, we looked at the criteria prospectively, the number of
patients, and we found that it was a marked variation in the prevalence between
winter and summer.

Norman Swan: With more being in summer.

Robert Moses: Yes. So compared to the autumn or spring there was about 25%
more women with abnormal results in summer, and 25% less in winter. So the
overall variation was about 50%.

Norman Swan: So the Canadian said, well, the reason for that is probably that
you are making insulin more efficient in winter because you are producing more
brown fat, but you don't agree with that conclusion.

Robert Moses: I don't think any of us have got down that far as to what the
possible reason is. Certainly, as I mentioned before, with a climate chamber and
controlling the ambient temperature from 20 through to 35 degrees there was a
dramatic increase in the glucose levels, not the fasting but the one and two hour
levels, starting at 25 to 30 degrees.

Norman Swan: But you think it could be a mistake in the way you are
measuring…not a mistake but an aberration in the way blood is shunted around
the body that might produce the result.

Robert Moses: As you say, it's not a mistake. The actual rise in the glucose level
was correlated with the core temperature. And what happens as you get a hotter
environment is that you tend to divert more blood from the arterial side to the
venous side so you can help to lose heat through the skin.

Norman Swan: And why should that affect your blood sugar?

Robert Moses: Because there's more glucose in the arterial side than in the
venous side because it hasn't gone through the small arterioles and things.

Norman Swan: So in other words what you are suggesting and what I saw in
your paper is that you could actually be over-diagnosing in summer. So it's not so
much that there's more gestational diabetes, it's just that the way you do the test
in that hotter temperature could actually give you a false positive result.

Robert Moses: Or a false negative in winter. So there is a 50% range…

Norman Swan: Not very comforting, Professor Moses.

Robert Moses: Well, we are about to embark with a climate chamber again,
looking at how long you have to be at a certain temperature before you don't
have this problem. It might be two hours or three hours, but that of course could
be a First World problem. You have to have air conditioning, et cetera. On the
other hand, if you go to places where this is not practical, you may have to devise
a correction factor to try and work out what the proper GTT…

Norman Swan: So what's a pregnant woman to do in the interim while you are
working it out?

Robert Moses: Well, I think that she should have her normal GTT at about 24 to
26 weeks, and then possibly discuss the results with whoever is looking after her.

Norman Swan: And work it out from there. We're sure to have you on when
you've got some more results from your chamber. Otherwise we can rest in our

belief, for the moment anyway, that brown fat may actually help you. Thanks for
joining us.

Robert Moses: It's a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Professor Bob Moses is director of the diabetes service at
Illawarra and Shoalhaven local health district. That's based in Wollongong.

Endometriosis is an incredibly common problem in women during their
childbearing years. It's hard to treat, causes infertility and a lot of pain. Here's
Olivia's story. It took nine years for Olivia to be diagnosed.

Olivia: First odd occurrence was getting my period at 10 years old, which is quite
young. It was around about when I was 14 that I started to notice that I was
suffering a lot more than the girls in my school. I thought maybe I was a bit of a
sook because I realised that I was having to take time off school and I was
bleeding for a lot longer and I was getting a lot of iron issues. My friends would
come up to me at school and say, oh, exercise really helps for period cramps.
And the first thing I thought was the last thing I can do at that time of the month is
exercise. I can't move, I can't get out of bed, and that's when I started to think
that there was something wrong.

So I had started going to the doctors as soon as I got heavy periods, they were
always saying, no, it's totally normal, it's fine, I'm sure it's not that bad, I'm sure
it's just a bad month. And I just listened to them as a young girl wanting to fix the
issue rather than create more issues. But it wasn't until early last year that I got
extraordinarily bad and the pains were insane and I started fainting quite
regularly and bled for about 10 weeks at a time. And I thought no, this isn't
normal. And so I pushed and pushed at several doctors, and finally got referred
to a gynaecologist who agreed and said, yes, you sound like textbook
endometriosis.

Then you need to have an operation to formally diagnose it, which is called a
laparoscopy. And you can choose a surgeon who is either an excision specialist
or just a regular gynaecologist. I would recommend an excision specialist
because they know how to look for endometriosis. And if it is, then usually during
that operation they will cut it out or burn it, called excision or ablation, and go

from there, which is hormone therapy or a plethora of other options, depending
on what your gynaecologist suggests.

Norman Swan: Olivia, who spoke to Joel Werner. As a result of recent genetic
research there are some women with endometriosis who may have more
effective options. For a condition with a very low risk of cancer, a North American
group has found surprisingly a set of cancer genes in endometriosis legions. One
of the team was Paul Yong who is a gynaecologist who specialises in
endometriosis at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver.

Paul Yong: One in 10 women of reproductive age have endometriosis, that's
approximately 1 million women in Canada.

Norman Swan: And 50% of women who have infertility have endometriosis.

Paul Yong: Yes, approximately half the women with infertility, approximately half
of women with troublesome pelvic pain have endometriosis.

Norman Swan: So how does a woman know she's got endometriosis? What's
the story?

Paul Yong: The symptoms include painful menstrual cramps, also painful sexual
activity, painful bowel movements, the latter often are worse at the time of the
period. There can also be pained that is there are even daily. And then a history
of infertility can often be suggested.

Norman Swan: And the pain is mostly in the pelvis?

Paul Yong: Mostly in the pelvis, yes.

Norman Swan: And what's going on here is that tissue from the uterus, from the
womb, gets seeded throughout the pelvis and sometimes throughout the bowel.

Paul Yong: Yes.

Norman Swan: And we don't know very much about it apart from the fact that
once a woman goes through menopause it tends to go away.

Paul Yong: That is correct, yes, it seems to be an oestrogen dependent disease.

Norman Swan: And where are we at with treatment for endometriosis? Because
there is not just one type.

Paul Yong: Treatment is primarily hormonal or surgical. Hormonal includes
progestin based therapies such as the birth control pill, or progesterone only
treatments. And then surgery involves excision or ablation of legions, or
hysterectomy.

Norman Swan: And there are mainly two kinds of lesion here with
endometriosis, aren't there, ones which are a bit superficial and attach to tissues,
and a type where it really burrows into the organ that it attaches itself to, which is
a bit like cancer except that it's not cancer.

Paul Yong: Correct, that's exactly it. The latter type has tumour-like qualities but
is most definitely benign and extremely rare for the deep infiltrating type of
endometriosis to be associated with cancer.

Norman Swan: Is there any relationship at all between endometriosis and
cancer?

Paul Yong: There is a relationship that appears with endometriosis that grows on
the ovary, which is the third subtype of endometriosis and certain subtypes of
ovarian cancer. It's about a 2 to 4 fold increase in risk. But because
endometriosis is so common, only a very tiny fraction of women with
endometriosis develop cancer.

Norman Swan: And what do we know about what causes it or the risk factors
that put a woman at risk of endometriosis?

Paul Yong: There seems to be some factors based on ethnicity, for example,
and there are gene changes that one inherits that could potentially be dietary
factors or other environmental factors…

Norman Swan: Such as?

Paul Yong: A lot of them are not in a total confirmed state, so I would hesitate to
say for sure.

Norman Swan: And the ethnic groups?

Paul Yong: It's thought that Caucasians may have a higher rate of
endometriosis.

Norman Swan: So this was a genetic study. You talked about inherited genes
there that might put you at added risk, but this is a study not of inherited genes
but of the genes that might be mutated in women with endometriosis, particularly
of this deep infiltrating kind, it's something new to the endometriosis itself.

Paul Yong: Yes.

Norman Swan: A small study, but tell us briefly what he found.

Paul Yong: What we found is that this subtype of endometriosis, the cells
contain gene changes or mutations in certain genes that have been seen to be
involved in a certain type of cancer. So these are gene mutations that are
thought to drive cancer cell growth or invasion. So we found these same gene
mutations in endometriosis, the deep infiltrating subtype. So again, this subtype
is very rare to become cancer, so what we think is that these gene mutations
may be driving how endometriosis cells can grow or become invasive in some
areas, and that could fundamentally change management.

Norman Swan: There's quite a spread though in these mutations, it wasn't
consistent, it wasn't the same mutation in every woman.

Paul Yong: Correct, yes, different between individuals.

Norman Swan: Why might that be?

Paul Yong: That's a really good question. It's not completely clear. I think one
factor is that the technologies for detecting these mutations are evolving, and we
think that there will be even more mutations detected with more sensitive
techniques. The other factor is that although there are several different genes
seen, all of them potentially confer an advantage on the cells to be able to grow.

Norman Swan: In cancer, you get these mutations because of environmental
factors…sorry to keep on coming back to this. So, for example, in melanoma
where some of these mutations occur, it's sunlight. In colon cancer it could be red
meat or toxins in the bowel. In the lung it can be tobacco smoke or unknown

environmental factors. It's going to be an environmental factor that induces these
mutations in the endometriosis, surely?

Paul Yong: Yes, I think that is a fantastic point and I think definitely more work is
needed to find these environmental factors that are involved in mutations or
healthy cells and mutations survive longer. There's a different study that looked
at some other benign conditions that carry these type of mutations and they
found that age, so increased age was a factor, and I believe smoking was also a
factor. But I don't think that can be extrapolated to endometriosis but I think…

Norman Swan: No, because it's a young woman's disease. And finally, at least
one of these mutations, the KRAS gene, has drugs which are available to treat it
if it's cancer. Surely it's worth trying those on endometriosis, isn't it?

Paul Yong: Yes, there is definitely a lot of potential there for sure. The KRAS
iteration, as far as I know, it's been a somewhat difficult target. So the drugs look
at I believe downstream targets of the KRAS gene. But we would be very
interested in the endometriosis that carries this mutation for specific drugs and
increase the number of treatment options for women.

Norman Swan: So a woman listening to this will wonder should she ask for gene
testing if she's got endometriosis. Is there any point at the moment?

Paul Yong: At this point we don't know the full clinical implications of these gene
mutations, so we are actively working on that right now to see whether these
mutations influence pain levels or infertility, or where endometriosis grows, for
example, or whether a woman will respond to hormonal treatment or surgery. So
all of those are unknowns right now. And until we know that, mutation testing
would be just part of our research protocol.

Norman Swan: Paul Yong, thank you very much for joining us on the Health
Report.

Paul Yong: Thank you very much for having me.

Norman Swan: Paul Yong is in the BC Women's Centre for Pelvic Pain and
Endometriosis in Vancouver.

Hip and knee replacements for arthritis are, in the right circumstances, highly
effective operations. They can restore mobility and reduce pain. And because of
that, joint replacement surgery is increasingly being used in younger men and
women. The big question though is whether by having a joint replacement at a
younger age you increase your chances of needing it to be revised. In other
words, a repeat operation, which the evidence suggests is rarely as good as the
first operation.

There is a register of joint replacements in Australia, but it and other national
registries have not been good at estimating the lifetime risk of joint revision, and
that's what a study published recently in the Lancet has done, looking at the
effect of age at first total joint replacement on the risk of subsequent revision.
The first author was orthopaedic surgeon Lee Bayliss of the University of Oxford.
Welcome to the Health Report.

Lee Bayliss: Thank you for having me.

Norman Swan: Just tell us about the study, because it was pretty big.

Lee Bayliss: Yes, so this is based on a primary care dataset which includes
something in the region of 6 million patients. And so within that we had access to
just over 120,000 patients who had had a first time hip or knee replacement, and
that was over a period of approximately 20 years.

Norman Swan: As opposed to, say, the Australian National Joint Replacement
Registry which goes for a year or maybe 10 years, so it's a much longer period of
time.

Lee Bayliss: Yes, sure, and similarly with our own national registry which is over
10 years now by some way but still limited to that time period. So the benefit of
this study was having a more protracted time course to follow these patients that
had these joint replacements and to be able to see what variations there were in
terms of how quickly and at what time following their first procedure they needed
to have that joint replacement really replaced, as you say, a revision procedure.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Lee Bayliss: What we found was that the extremes of age, so about 15% each
of patients having joint replacements are under 60 and over 80, so those two
groups together constitute about a third of patients, and they displayed very
different behaviours. So I think the most important thing really is that the patients
over 70, in both men and women and hip and knee replacements, the chances of
requiring a second operation within your lifespan were 5%, something in the
region of one in 20.

Norman Swan: If you're over 70.

Lee Bayliss: If you're over 70. And then by contrast of that, if you are under 60,
and particularly the youngest age group, the 50 to 54 age group, there is a
significant increase in the risk of a requirement for a second operation…

Norman Swan: Sorry, we lost you for a moment there. So the 50 year group,
what was their revisionary…?

Lee Bayliss: Yes, 50 to 54, that was the highest risk of revision for both men and
women, significantly more so in men where the revision risk went up something
like one in three, and around 35% for men having knee replacements and a little
bit less for men having hip replacements. But significantly less for women but still
the highest risk for women was in the youngest age groups.

Norman Swan: And you found that the median time to revision for patients who
had surgery younger than 60 was 4.4 years.

Lee Bayliss: Yes, we did…

Norman Swan: So is that in that 30% who needed a revision, or overall?

Lee Bayliss: That's a function of the population. So yes, as you say, of those
people that needed revision, they had it within that time period. But what we also
found is when we looked at something called the hazard function, so the chance
of you needing a revision at any given point in time, so whatever number of days
or years following your surgery, your risk at that point in time of requiring a
second operation, what we found was that was consistently higher in the in the
youngest patients, be they male or female, hip or knee replacement patients. And
I think previously we probably would have not expected that to necessarily have

been the case consistently throughout the course of those younger patients, but
that's what our data showed.

Norman Swan: We are running out of time, so just very brief questions. Not
much difference between hips and knees, knees a bit worse than the hips
basically you found, is that right?

Lee Bayliss: No, hips are slightly worse than knees overall.

Norman Swan: Oh really? Why men more than women in the other group?

Lee Bayliss: Really difficult to answer. The honest answer is that wasn't in the
scope of the study, and I can speculate that the traditional reasons that people
give tends to be to do with body weight and profession. But again, that
speculation rather than anything we looked into in this study.

Norman Swan: What the Australian register has shown is that the older hip joints
and the cheaper ones have been the most reliable ones and the newer ones less
reliable. Did you find any cohort effect? There's been some spectacularly
unreliable hip joints. Did you find any difference by year?

Lee Bayliss: No. We did look. What we did not have was data on the proprietary
implants. I imagine you're talking about metal or metal implants. We didn't have
any information about specific types of implants, it was just total hip or a total
knee. Looking across the time periods, the revision rates for both hip and knee
were relatively uniform.

Norman Swan: So the message is, Lee, 'hang on if you can'.

Lee Bayliss: Well, that's difficult to answer because obviously this is looking at a
population, not an individual patient's course through those ages. I think it's just
important that patients enter into discussion about whether they're going to have
a joint replacement or not are fully versed as best they can be in the risks of that
procedure.

Norman Swan: Lee Bayliss of the University of Oxford, thanks very much for
joining us.

Lee Bayliss: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Lee Bayliss is in the department of orthopaedics, rheumatology
and musculoskeletal science at the University of Oxford. I'm Norman Swan, this
has been the Health Report, hope to see you next week.
